steps.title: If you opened a file or allowed remote access, unplug that computer
steps.detail: Unplug its network cable and turn off Wi-Fi. Leave it switched on. If you only clicked a link and typed nothing, keep going with the next steps.
steps.why: Cutting the network stops an attacker who may be connected through that computer. Leaving it on keeps evidence for your IT contact.
steps.do_not: Do not keep using that computer for email, banking or passwords.

steps.title: Change the password from a clean device
steps.detail: If you typed a password on the fake page, change it now from your phone or another computer that shows no warning. Use a new, long password you have not used before.
steps.why: The attacker may already have the old password. Changing it first locks them out.
steps.source_name: FTC: How to recognize and avoid phishing scams
steps.do_not: Do not change it from the computer where you clicked.

steps.title: Turn on two-step verification
steps.detail: In the account settings, turn on two-step verification (a code from an app or a text message). Do it for email first, then banking.
steps.why: Even with your password, an attacker cannot sign in without the second step.

steps.title: Change the same password everywhere you used it
steps.detail: List every account where you used that password, the same or almost the same. Change each one, starting with email, bank and payroll.
steps.why: Attackers try a stolen password on many sites. One reused password can open several accounts.

steps.title: Sign out other sessions and check recovery details
steps.detail: In the account security page, sign out of all other devices. Check that the recovery email and phone number are yours.
steps.why: An attacker who is already signed in can stay in after a password change, and can change recovery details to take the account back.

steps.title: Ask your IT contact to check the mailbox
steps.detail: Ask them to look for forwarding rules, unknown sign-ins and messages you did not send.
steps.why: Attackers often add hidden rules that forward or delete mail, so you do not see warnings.

steps.title: Call your IT contact
steps.detail: Tell them what you clicked, what you typed and when. Ask them to scan the computer and check other accounts.
steps.why: They can check whether malware was installed and whether other computers are affected.

steps.title: If a pop-up or caller says they are tech support, stop
steps.detail: Close the pop-up or hang up. Real companies do not call you out of the blue or lock your screen to ask you to call.
steps.why: Fake support scams try to get remote access, passwords or payment.
steps.do_not: Do not call the number on the pop-up and do not let anyone you do not know connect to your computer.

steps.title: If you gave card or bank details, or paid, call your bank
steps.detail: Call the fraud line on the back of your card or on your contacts card. Ask them to block the card and watch the account.
steps.why: Banks can block cards and sometimes reverse payments if they know quickly.
steps.source_name: FTC: What to do if you were scammed
steps.do_not: Do not wait to see if money goes missing.

steps.title: Warn your staff about the message
steps.detail: Tell staff what the message looked like and that they should not click it. Ask anyone who clicked to tell you now.
steps.why: Phishing emails are often sent to several people at once. Others may have the same message.

steps.title: Keep the message and write down what happened
steps.detail: Keep the email or text. Take a photo of the fake page if it is still open. Write down the time, what you clicked and what you typed.
steps.why: Your IT contact, bank and the police will need these details.
steps.do_not: Do not forward the email to staff as a warning: describe it instead.

steps.title: Report it
steps.detail: In the US, report it at reportfraud.ftc.gov. If money was lost, also report it to the FBI at ic3.gov.
steps.why: Reports help stop the same attackers and may be needed by your bank or insurer.

steps.title: Outside the US? Report it in your country
steps.detail: In Canada, report it to the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security at cyber.gc.ca and to your local police. In France, get help at cybermalveillance.gouv.fr.
steps.why: National services can help you report the crime and recover.
